rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the eight-peak elution window while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. This provides a baseline for identifying critical pairs and trimming the gradient window.

Halve the gradient slope while keeping the solvent endpoints and temperature fixed to identify which crowded pairs respond to slope. All eight peaks eluted early in the first run, leaving room to test a shallower gradient.
Test whether higher temperature separates the remaining critical pair while bringing the last peak below 10 minutes. Keeping the gradient unchanged isolates the temperature effect.
The temperature change resolved the original crowded cluster but created a new co-elution at 60 C. Testing 55 C should separate that new pair while retaining most of the time savings.
At 60 C, all but one pair were fully resolved. A modestly steeper gradient tests whether that co-elution can be separated while keeping the final peak comfortably below 10 minutes.

The critical pair improved when tG decreased from 24 to 22 minutes. Extending that trend to 18 minutes may bring it near baseline resolution, while testing the remaining resolution margins in the other pairs.

Injection 6 is nearly optimal, with only one pair just below R = 1.5. Raise the starting organic fraction while preserving its gradient slope to test a small selectivity shift and shorten retention without broadly compressing the separation.

Use a slightly shallower slope than injection 7 to improve its two early critical pairs. The later close pairs retain some resolution margin, so this small adjustment targets full resolution with the final peak still below 10 minutes.

Reduce the slope slightly from 0.0464 to 0.045 organic fraction per minute, targeting R ≥ 1.5 for both early critical pairs while preserving the later pair’s margin. The final organic fraction remains comfortably above the observed elution window.

Injection 9 achieved the maximum CRF; now test a shorter separation by raising the starting organic fraction. Keeping the endpoint and duration fixed makes the slope shallower, which may compensate for the loss of early-pair resolution at a higher starting fraction.

Retain injection 9 as the maximum-score method and explore lower-temperature selectivity for an alternative fully resolved separation. Using the gradient from injection 6 provides a direct temperature comparison with a reasonable chance of keeping all peaks near the 10-minute target.
Increase temperature one step from injection 11 to test whether its single unresolved pair improves while shortening retention. Injection 9 remains the established maximum-score method.

Test a shallower gradient to improve the unresolved middle pair seen at 25 C, while raising the starting organic fraction to offset the added retention time. Injection 9 remains the maximum-score reference.

Continue the improvement seen at 25 C by making the gradient shallower to resolve the remaining middle pair. Raising the starting organic fraction should offset much of the added retention and keep the final peak near or below 10 minutes.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step while preserving the slope of the fully resolved 25 C method. This tests whether its resolution margin can support a shorter separation without sacrificing the maximum CRF.

Combine a slightly shallower slope with a 5 C temperature increase to improve the remaining middle pair. Earlier low-temperature runs suggest warming helps this pair, while also offsetting the retention increase from the shallower gradient.

Return to 25 C to avoid the new early co-elution and reduce the slope from injection 15 to improve its unresolved middle pair. This targets another fully resolved method below 10 minutes; injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Raise the starting organic fraction to shorten the fully resolved separation from injection 17, while slightly reducing the slope to protect its critical middle pair. The maximum CRF is already secured, so this tests a faster alternative.

Raise temperature by 5 C to improve the sole unresolved middle pair and shorten the run. The preceding pair now has substantially more resolution margin than in earlier 30 C tests, making this a promising route to full resolution.

Make injection 19 slightly shallower to improve its sole unresolved pair, which showed little response to temperature. The neighboring pairs have some margin, and the last peak should remain below 10 minutes.

Keep the shallower slope that resolved the middle pair, but return to 25 C to restore separation of the final pair. The observed temperature response suggests the last peak should still elute below 10 minutes.

Return to the fastest maximum-score region and make injection 10’s gradient shallower to improve its early unresolved pair. This tests whether the higher starting organic fraction can deliver full resolution faster than injection 9, while checking the later pair’s remaining margin.

Test a small slope increase from the fastest fully resolved method, injection 9, to shorten retention while probing its narrow early-pair resolution margin. This slope lies between injection 9 and the slightly under-resolved injection 8.

Injection 23 indicates that further steepening the fastest fully resolved method sacrifices early-pair resolution. Test lower-temperature selectivity with injection 22’s gradient as an alternative route to full resolution, retaining injection 9 as the maximum-score reference.

Use the final injection for a slightly shallower slope than injection 9, testing whether its narrow early-pair margins improve without losing full resolution of the later pair. Injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed method attaining the maximum CRF of 1.000.
